_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a2.1: Rav: who does not establish our mishna in accordance with the Rabbis, holds in accordance with Reish Lakish, who said there [in Temura]: according to the Rabbis, items consecrated for Temple maintenance, etc. Therefore the mishna cannot be established entirely in accordance with the Rabbis.
rashi:a2.2: As the latter clause teaches: of our mishna, “if they died they must be buried,” since items consecrated for the altar were included in standing and valuation.
rashi:a3.1: If so: that the reason of the mishna is because [one may not redeem] consecrated animals [to feed them] to dogs.
rashi:a3.2: Let it teach: If they became tereifa they must be buried: which would imply that even though one could perform standing and valuation with them, they must be buried, since they are fit only for dogs. And since it took the case of “they died,” learn from this that the reason is standing and valuation. [The printed text has a bracketed “and not”:] unlike Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said there that according to the Rabbis both items consecrated for the altar and items consecrated for Temple maintenance were included; [according to him] the latter clause of the mishna can be established in accordance with the Rabbis, and the first clause too can be established according to them, since with an animal blemished from the outset everyone agrees, and one would teach: This is the statement of Rabbi Shimon and those who disagree with him.
rashi:a5.1: Gazelle: “as the gazelle and the hart.” And we establish in the Sifrei that the verse speaks of disqualified consecrated animals that were redeemed.
rashi:a5.2: Just as a gazelle and a hart are exempt from the firstborn: since “of your herd and of your flock” is written [regarding the firstborn].
rashi:a6.1: And I will not exclude the gifts: and below it asks what makes the gifts stronger than the firstborn.
rashi:a6.2: A gazelle and a hart are exempt from the gifts: since it is written regarding the gifts: “whether it be ox or sheep” (Deuteronomy 18:3).
rashi:a8.1: And what is different: about the gifts, that they are not excluded by the first term [“gazelle”]?
rashi:a8.2: And he answers: I will exclude the firstborn, which does not apply equally to all: since it does not apply to females as it does to males.
rashi:a9.1: A gazelle and a hart: [the prohibition of] itself and its offspring does not apply to a gazelle and a hart, since it is written: “whether it be ox or sheep” (Leviticus 22:28).
rashi:a10.1: He said to him: To what are you comparing it: the disqualified consecrated animals, that you would exempt them from itself and its offspring? Itself and its offspring applies to non-sacred animals and to consecrated ones, as is explained in Sheḥitat Ḥullin (Ḥullin 78a).
rashi:a11.1: If so, with regard to its fat as well: why was “however” needed to forbid it? Derive that it is forbidden [by the same reasoning]: “To what are you comparing them,” since you say that even though they are juxtaposed to the gazelle and the hart, they do not leave the category of consecrated animals.
rashi:a12.1: “However,” and not itself and its offspring: and it is reasonable that the juxtaposition comes to exempt them from the firstborn and the gifts, and “however” to forbid its fat and [to apply] itself and its offspring, for this way we compare them to fully consecrated animals; whereas if we said the reverse, we would compare them neither to consecrated animals nor to non-sacred ones.
rashi:a13.1: Only its blood: is written with regard to a blemished firstborn.
rashi:a15.1: The juxtaposition is effective: that they are juxtaposed to the gazelle and the hart.
rashi:a15.2: And the verse is effective: which would have been written, “You shall not eat its fat.” The juxtaposition would be effective [to exempt] from karet, and the reasoning would seem quite sound, since where karet is written for fat, it is written of an animal fit for an offering, as it is written: “For whoever eats the fat [of the animal of which men offer an offering]…” (Leviticus 7:25). And the verse would be effective to establish a prohibition for it, so that you would not permit it entirely. Therefore it expressed it, etc. [in the language of “its blood”].
rashi:a18.1: But didn’t the tanna: of the baraita above derive its fat from “however”? How then can Rava say that “however” comes for itself and its offspring?
rashi:a19.1: Had it not been stated, etc.: and what it teaches, “The verse states: ‘However,’ which differentiates,” means this: even if the verse had not written [“its blood”], I could exclude [its fat] from here.
rashi:a20.1: “Notwithstanding, after all the desire of your soul, you may slaughter and eat” (Deuteronomy 12:15): and we established it as speaking of disqualified consecrated animals after their redemption.
tosafot:a2.1: [This comment belongs further on.] Rav holds in accordance with Reish Lakish: at the end of Temura it is implied so, since Rav Giddel says that Rav says: “What is the reason of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish?”
tosafot:a6.1: In brief: Just as a gazelle and a hart are exempt from the firstborn and from the gifts: Our passage implies that without “however” we would also expound that, as with a gazelle and a hart, itself and its offspring does not apply and the fat is permitted; and at the end of chapter 1 (Bekhorot 12a) we also expound: just as a gazelle and a hart are not redeemed, so disqualified consecrated animals are not redeemed. This is puzzling: from where do we derive all these expositions, when “gazelle and hart” is written three times and each is needed for something else, as explained in chapter Pesulei HaMukdashin (Bekhorot 33a)? One may answer that there too one is explained for the firstborn and the gifts, as here, one from “gazelle” and one from “hart.” Another is explained there for the statement of Rabbi Yitzḥak and Rabbi Oshaya, as Rabbeinu Tam explains: one who mates or drives an ox of disqualified consecrated animals is flogged, since they are one body and the verse made them two bodies, like driving a gazelle and a hart together, so he is liable for diverse kinds. Another is for Rabbi Akiva, who permits [feeding them] even to a gentile, or for Rabbi Elazar HaKappar (Ḥullin 28a): just as disqualified consecrated animals require slaughter, so do a gazelle and a hart; and from “gazelle” alone we would have known “hart,” since from “gazelle” we derive every undomesticated animal. The last is for Rav Mari. As for “just as a gazelle and a hart are not redeemed,” “its fat is permitted” and “itself and its offspring,” which the Gemara would expound but for “however”: these come from the same “gazelle and hart” from which we expound the firstborn and the gifts, which shows that the verse wishes to give them the status of an undomesticated animal, and “however” is written to make one liable for its fat and for itself and its offspring, as explained [by Abaye]: whether you compare them to non-sacred animals or to consecrated ones. And shortly, where it asks about their offspring and their milk, “If conceived and born after their redemption, it is the offspring of a gazelle and a hart,” no extra verse is involved; it is simply obvious to the Gemara that such an animal is entirely like a gazelle and a hart. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a9.1: If so, just as itself and its offspring does not apply to a gazelle and a hart: he could not ask: just as a gazelle and a hart require covering [of the blood], so too disqualified consecrated animals, since we explicitly expound in chapter Kisui HaDam (Ḥullin 84a), regarding disqualified consecrated animals: “You shall pour it upon the earth like water” (Deuteronomy 12:24): just as, etc. [water requires no covering, so their blood requires none].
tosafot:a13.1: Only you shall not eat its blood: this verse is written regarding a firstborn, and it is very puzzling that he does not cite “Only you shall not eat the blood,” which is written regarding other disqualified consecrated animals. And one cannot object that perhaps that verse is needed for the five prohibitions stated about blood, which are explained in chapter 1 of Keritot (4b), since many more than five prohibitions are written: one in Vayikra, one in Tzav et Aharon, two in Aḥarei Mot and four in Re’eh, which is eight besides this one of the firstborn. Perhaps he expounds them for something else.
tosafot:a17.1: And the verse is effective, to establish a prohibition for it: And if you ask: on the contrary, since the verse brings it back [to its prohibition], it brings it back completely, even to karet, as is taught below regarding disqualified consecrated animals: one who shears or works them incurs the forty [lashes]; and it does not say that since they are juxtaposed to a gazelle and a hart this removes them entirely from the prohibition, so that “you may slaughter, but not shear” would be a mere prohibition; rather it says that [the verse] restored them to their prohibition. One must distinguish. And from that [baraita], “one who shears or works them,” there is also a difficulty for what was explained, that a flavor without its substance is forbidden but one is not flogged for it, as with gentiles’ vessels [that require purging]: since a detrimental flavor was permitted, like a putrid carcass, when [the Torah] again forbade gentiles’ vessels in Midian there would be only a mere prohibition, not lashes. And this does not seem right, since you must say that it restored it to its prohibition, as I explained.
gershom:a1.1: [The Sages] said: Rav holds in accordance with Reish Lakish, who said at the end of tractate Temura: according to the Rabbis, items consecrated for Temple maintenance were included [in standing and valuation]; items consecrated for the altar were not.
gershom:a2.1: And it cannot be established: this mishna of Bekhorot in accordance with the Rabbis, because of the latter clause, which teaches: “But if their consecration preceded their blemish, if they died they must be buried.” If it were the Rabbis, since they say that items consecrated for the altar were not [included], it should have taught: “If they died they may be redeemed.” But in accordance with Rabbi Shimon both the first clause and the latter clause can be established, since he said that items consecrated for the altar were included; therefore when their consecration preceded their blemish they must be buried, but with an animal blemished from the outset, that is, whose blemish preceded its consecration, he concedes that it is redeemed. According to the Rabbis, though, it should have [said] that both this and that are redeemed.
gershom:a3.1: [The Sages] say: one can still establish it in accordance with the Rabbis, who say that items consecrated for the altar were not [included]. For from where [do you know] that what is taught, “if they died they must be buried,” is because they require standing and valuation where their consecration preceded their blemish, which is impossible since they died?
gershom:a4.1: Perhaps: according to the Rabbis too, even though they say that items consecrated for the altar were not [included], we say they must be buried for this reason: that one may not redeem sacrificial animals, etc. But where their blemish preceded their consecration they are redeemed, since such an animal is not considered so fully consecrated.
gershom:a5.1: [The Sages] said: If so, that they must be buried for this reason, because one may not redeem [sacrificial animals to feed them to] dogs, let it teach: “If they became tereifa they must be buried,” which would imply that even though they are still alive and it is possible to stand and value them, they must nevertheless be buried, because one may not redeem [to feed] dogs. But since it speaks of after death, “if they died they must be buried,” learn from this that it is because they were included in standing and valuation; so it is established in accordance with Rabbi Shimon and not the Rabbis.
gershom:a6.1: And if you wish, say: actually it can be established in accordance with the Rabbis too, and Rav holds in accordance with Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said in the last chapter of Temura that according to the Rabbis both items consecrated for the altar and items consecrated for Temple maintenance were included, and they concede regarding animals blemished from the outset. If so, he should have taught: “This is the statement of Rabbi Shimon and those who disagree with him.” Yes, he did indeed teach so.
gershom:a7.1: From where are these matters derived: that disqualified consecrated animals whose consecration preceded their blemish are exempt from the firstborn and from the gifts?
gershom:a8.1: As the Sages taught: “However, as the gazelle and the hart are eaten”: just as a gazelle is exempt from the firstborn, since it is written: “[every firstborn] male [that is born] of your herd and of your flock you shall sanctify” (Deuteronomy 15:19), and not of a gazelle.
gershom:a9.1: So too disqualified consecrated animals are exempt: for this passage speaks of disqualified consecrated animals, since it is written: “the impure and the pure [may eat of it]” (Deuteronomy 12:22). Even though they are disqualified consecrated animals, since their consecration preceded their blemish they still have sanctity, and they are exempt from the firstborn, since they were consecrated with sanctity of the body before they became blemished.
gershom:a10.1: I will exclude the firstborn: that they are exempt from the firstborn; and I will not exclude the gifts: rather, they are obligated in the gifts.
gershom:a11.1: And what is different: that they would be exempt from the firstborn and obligated in the gifts? If you say it is because the firstborn is more lenient, since it does not apply equally to all, as a firstborn is only a male, whereas the gifts apply both to males and to females: the verse states “hart.” That is why “hart” is written, [to teach] that it is exempt, since it is written: “whether it be ox or sheep… and he shall give to the priest,” etc. (Deuteronomy 18:3).
gershom:a12.1: The verse states “however”: it excludes disqualified consecrated animals, [teaching] that their fat is forbidden.
gershom:a13.1: He said to him: To what are you comparing them? If you exempt them from the firstborn and the gifts, you compare them to fully consecrated animals; and when you obligate in the firstborn and the gifts those whose permanent blemish preceded their consecration, you compare them to fully non-sacred animals. But if you exempt them from itself and its offspring, you compare them neither to consecrated animals nor to non-sacred ones.
gershom:a14.1: If so: with its fat too, “however” should not be needed to exclude it, since we would also say: to what are you comparing them?
gershom:a15.1: [A note printed with Rabbeinu Gershom: from his words it appears that his text did not read “Rather, didn’t you say…” but “Abaye said to him…”; perhaps our reading “Rather” is a scribal error for an abbreviation of “Abaye said to him,” as in Rabbeinu Gershom’s text, and that is correct.] Abaye: certainly what I said, “To what are you comparing them,” etc., is not a valid argument. Rather, this is what one can say: just as you said “however” and not their fat, so too say “however” and not itself and its offspring. [In this reading Abaye, not Rav Pappa, says this; the chat follows the Davidson translation.]
gershom:a16.1: Rather: what is the “its blood” that is forbidden here? Certainly it forbids only its fat.
gershom:a17.1: The juxtaposition is effective: that disqualified consecrated animals are juxtaposed to a gazelle and a hart, to exclude their fat from karet, just as there is no karet for the fat of a gazelle and a hart.
gershom:a18.1: And the verse is effective: “Only you shall not eat its blood,” to establish a mere prohibition for it, and not karet.
gershom:a19.1: For this reason: its fat is written in the language of “its blood,” to tell you: just as the blood of a gazelle is [punished] with karet, so too the fat of disqualified consecrated animals is with karet.
gershom:a20.1: But didn’t the tanna say “however,” and not its fat: and it is not derived from “its blood.”
rashi:b1.1: Some say: “You may slaughter and eat,” etc.: from here [this version] derives that shearing and milk are forbidden; “flesh” is the ordinary way of the verse and is not expounded, and it does not expound “and eat” to exclude dogs.
rashi:b2.1: Rather, where it was conceived before their redemption and born after their redemption: therefore they are forbidden, and they have no sanctity, neither to be sacrificed nor for their value, as is explained below: “What will be with them?”
rashi:b2.2: But before their redemption: if they were born [then], they are also sacred.
rashi:b3.1: From where are these matters derived: that if they were born before their redemption they are sacred?
rashi:b3.2: “Male,” to include the offspring: regarding peace offerings it is written (Leviticus 3:1): “whether male or female, without blemish,” and it is an extra verse. For let the verse be silent about it: since it did not fix “male” for it as it fixed for the burnt offering, it would follow that a female too is fit. Why then do I need “male” [and “female”]? To include the offspring of a peace offering. And if you ask: derive it from “which you have” (Deuteronomy 12:26)? Answer: it is a dispute of tanna’im; there is one who derives it from here and one who derives it from there, and so it is explained in tractate Temura, chapter Elu Kodashim (Temura 17b).
rashi:b4.1: The offspring of unblemished animals: the offspring of an unblemished animal.
rashi:b4.2: The offspring of blemished animals: (and all of them) whose consecration preceded their blemish.
rashi:b5.1: Those offspring of after their redemption: born [after], and conceived before their redemption: what will be with them? For they are fit neither in themselves nor for their value, as Rav Huna explains.
rashi:b5.2: Those born before their redemption, they disagree about them: about what we said above, “whether male,” to include the offspring of blemished animals.
rashi:b5.3: There is one who says: in tractate Temura, chapter Elu Kodashim (ibid.): they are sacred to be sacrificed.
rashi:b5.4: And there is one who says they are sacred for grazing: until they become blemished and are sold, and their money goes to [purchase] freewill offerings.
rashi:b6.1: One gathers them into a kippa: into a chamber, and they die of hunger.
rashi:b6.2: Deferred sanctity: for they have two flaws: one, that their mothers were blemished, [fit] at first and then deferred; and further, that they were born after redemption. And one cannot transfer them to full sanctity to be sacrificed, since once they were deferred they are no longer fit.
rashi:b6.3: It is not strong enough to transfer their redemption: their sanctity [is not strong enough], so that they would go out to non-sacred status, since their sanctity already went out through their mother’s redemption; for the fact that they are forbidden is a mere decree, as below. By Torah law, a fetus is [like] its mother’s thigh, and its sanctity lapsed with its mother’s redemption, as we said above about sanctity of value, that its offspring is permitted after redemption. Sanctity of the body is no different, since there is no distinction between sanctity of the body and sanctity of value with regard to redemption, except that this one requires a blemish and that one does not.
rashi:b7.1: Is that to say that they are fit for redemption: this is said in astonishment. That is, can the term “redemption” apply to them before he dedicates them? [Surely not,] for they are not strong enough!
rashi:b7.2: Close to their mother’s redemption one dedicates them for the sake of that same offering: for now sanctity takes effect on them in their own right, since he had them in mind, and their sanctity does not lapse through their mother’s redemption; and he waits until they become blemished and redeems them.
rashi:b7.3: And what is the reason: [that] Rav Huna said they are put to death, and they are not given a remedy as Rabbi Ḥanina [gives]?
rashi:b7.4: Rabbi Levi said: They decreed, etc.: If you say that the offspring have a remedy, one will come to raise flocks of disqualified consecrated animals: when a blemish falls on a consecrated animal he will not redeem it, and he will come to eat [the offspring] without redemption. But when we cause the offspring to be lost, he hastens to redeem the mother as soon as a blemish falls on it. [So I received] from Rabbi Eliezer, by word of mouth and in his responsum. Another version: both according to the one who says they are put to death and according to the one who says one dedicates them, what is the reason the Rabbis put him to such trouble instead of leaving them in their prohibition? It is a decree lest he raise flocks upon flocks, which will bear offspring, and those offspring other offspring, and he will come to a stumbling-block through them. But once he has redeemed them it does not matter if they give birth, since they are the offspring of a gazelle and a hart. Another version, and it is the main one, from the mouth of the teacher: “And what is the reason” refers back to our mishna: why are [the offspring] forbidden after their mother’s redemption, when their sanctity lapsed with their mother’s redemption, just as it lapses with sanctity of value, whose offspring is permitted after redemption, as said above? It is a decree lest one raise flocks from disqualified consecrated animals that are redeemed, for the sake of the offspring born after redemption, and come through them to shearing and labor. But above, regarding [animals] whose blemish preceded their consecration, we do not decree, because it is an uncommon matter, as we say in tractate Temura (6b): one who dedicates blemished animals for the altar transgresses five prohibitions. And with those whose consecration preceded their blemish themselves, we permit [offspring] conceived and born after their redemption and do not decree, since once you have forbidden those conceived before their redemption, he will not come to put off [redeeming] them.
rashi:b8.1: May one dedicate them: those offspring in the womb of disqualified consecrated animals, for any offering he wishes?
rashi:b8.2: He may not dedicate them: except for that same offering.
rashi:b8.3: “Within your gates”: is written about a firstborn: “And if there be any blemish therein… you shall eat it within your gates” (Deuteronomy 15:21–22); and about disqualified consecrated animals it is written: “in all your gates which [the Lord your God] gives you” (Deuteronomy 12:15).
rashi:b8.4: “Which is born as a firstborn… no man shall sanctify it”: evidently no other sanctity takes effect on it.
rashi:b9.1: And he does not incur the forty: even though shearing them before redemption is forbidden, he is not flogged for it, since “you shall not shear” is written of fully consecrated animals; but there is at least a prohibition, as with anyone who benefits from consecrated property.
rashi:b9.2: Whether before their redemption or after their redemption they do not render a substitute: since we require [an animal] good from the outset, as I explained above.
rashi:b10.1: Before their redemption one is liable for misuse with them: for he benefits from consecrated property, since they are no less than items consecrated for Temple maintenance.
rashi:b10.2: And their offspring are non-sacred: even if they were conceived before their redemption and born after their redemption.
rashi:b10.3: And they are redeemed unblemished: if they were conceived and born before their redemption.
rashi:b10.4: You have with them only the mitzva of value alone: that one assesses them in money.
rashi:b11.1: And whether before their redemption or after their redemption they render a substitute: and below it says that a substitute made after their redemption must die.
rashi:b12.1: After their redemption one is not liable for misuse with them: since they are juxtaposed to a gazelle and a hart; but not with regard to shearing, since it is written: “you may slaughter,” but not shear.
rashi:b12.2: And their offspring are sacred: if they were conceived before their redemption.
rashi:b12.3: And one may not dedicate them as any offering he wishes: and this is [the view] of Rav Sheshet.
tosafot:b8.1: Just as one cannot dedicate a firstborn as any offering he wishes: that is, once it is born; but in its mother’s womb one can change it to another offering, as we learned in chapter Keitzad Ma’arimin (Temura 24b). Even so, we properly derive from it that the offspring of disqualified consecrated animals may not be changed to another offering even in their mothers’ womb, according to the one who says they are sacred in their mothers’ womb: just as one cannot change a firstborn once firstborn sanctity has taken effect on it, so too [the offspring of] disqualified consecrated animals, which are already sacred, cannot be changed to another offering. And even according to the one who says they become sacred only when they come into being, they are not like a firstborn before it is born, since these stand to become sacred by force of their mother, who is already sacred.
gershom:b1.1: Some say: “You may slaughter and eat flesh”: you have permission with them only from the time of slaughter onward, when it is fit to eat, but not before; [before then] you have no permission with them. Evidently they are forbidden for shearing and labor.
gershom:b2.1: But one may redeem sacrificial animals [to feed them to dogs]: since “and eat” is not extra for him to forbid it. And wherever we say, “This works well according to the one who says one may not redeem [to feed dogs], but according to the one who says one may redeem…,” it is from here that it is derived.
gershom:b3.1: Why? It is the offspring of a gazelle and a hart: that is, they are non-sacred.
gershom:b4.1: But born before their redemption, that is, before: for before [redemption] they are also sacred, as is said below: there is one who says they are sacred to be sacrificed, and there is one who says they are sacred for grazing.
gershom:b5.1: From where are these matters derived: that [offspring] born after his redemption are forbidden?
gershom:b6.1: As the Sages taught: “male”: “And if his offering be a sacrifice of peace offerings, if he offers of the herd,” etc. What need is there to say “whether male or female”? Don’t I know on my own that male and female are fit for a peace offering? Rather, “male” is to include the offspring, for “offspring” implies male and female; [“female”] is to include the substitute, for “substitute” implies female.
gershom:b7.1: [A note printed with Rabbeinu Gershom: it seems one should read, “and so it is in Temura (17b): Those offspring,” etc.] So it is written in Temura, etc.: those offspring after their redemption, which were conceived before their redemption and born after their redemption. For those conceived and born before their redemption, they disagree about them in Temura, chapter Elu Kodashim, regarding what we say, that these offspring and substitutes of blemished animals are sacred: Shmuel said they are sacred to be sacrificed, since they are unblemished and come by force of sanctity of the body, as they were born before redemption; and Bar Padda said they are sacred for grazing, since they are redeemed not unblemished but only blemished, and they are not sacred to be sacrificed, so that the secondary should not be more stringent than the primary. But those born after their redemption, what will be with them, etc.? They come by force of deferred sanctity, since their mothers had already been redeemed when they were born.
gershom:b8.1: It is not strong enough: their sanctity, to transfer to their redemption; and since they have no power to transfer, they too do not go out to non-sacred status. Therefore they die.
gershom:b9.1: [The Sages] said: this way they do have power to be redeemed: for close to the redemption of the offspring, before he redeems them, he dedicates them for the sake of that same offering; that is, he consecrates them for the sake of their mother’s offering, and that consecration helps them come to redemption.
gershom:b10.1: Is that to say that they are fit for redemption: that they have the power to be dedicated for the sake of that same offering? But we said they are not strong enough to transfer!
gershom:b11.1: Rather, close to their mother’s redemption: that is, while they are fetuses, before the offspring are born, he dedicates them along with their mother for the sake of their mother’s offering, and through this they have sanctity [strong enough] to transfer to their redemption.
gershom:b12.1: What is the reason: that one must take the trouble in these matters so that they come to redemption?
gershom:b13.1: A decree lest one raise flocks of them: and come to a stumbling-block, if a person eats of them or sacrifices them.
gershom:b14.1: Just as one cannot dedicate a firstborn as any offering he wishes, as it is written: “But the firstborn… no man shall sanctify it”: that is, for the sake of another offering.
gershom:b15.1: So too: the offspring of disqualified consecrated animals, etc.
gershom:b16.1: Whether before their redemption or after their redemption, one who shears or works them does not incur the forty: And if you say: but we learned in the mishna that after redemption they are permitted, which implies that before [redemption] they are not, this is not difficult: here too it teaches only that he does not incur [the lashes], but there is at least a prohibition.
gershom:b17.1: And their offspring are non-sacred: after their redemption.
gershom:b18.1: And they are redeemed: even unblemished.
gershom:b19.1: Only the mitzva of value: that is, the stringency that they require redemption.
gershom:b20.1: But if [their consecration] preceded, etc.: the “whether before or after” said here is needed only because he said it in the first clause, so he said it in the latter clause too.
gershom:b21.1: Their offspring are sacred: [those] conceived before redemption and born after their redemption.
gershom:b22.1: The principle of the matter in the latter clause comes to include its fat: that it is forbidden to eat, as we say, “You may slaughter and eat,” etc. And one cannot say it comes to include one who slaughters them outside, that he is liable, for we could say that one who slaughters them outside is also exempt, since their blood would not be accepted inside, as they come by force of deferred sanctity, the mothers having already been redeemed. [The Gemara on 16a reads: to include its milk.]
